summary: Nanjing University authors rename identifiers in a semantics-preserving way: similar names, placeholders like var0, or names borrowed from an unrelated 'donor' snippet. They measure four snippet-level tasks (code-doc matching, code search and summarization on 600 CodeSearchNet samples; completion on HumanEval) across GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini, Llama3-70B, DeepSeek-Coder-V2, text-embedding-3 and small fine-tuned encoders. Scores fall as names become uninformative and fall most when names mislead; for example, GPT-3.5 two-choice code-doc selection drops from 92.8% to 52.4% and text-embedding-3 search MRR from 91.5 to 47.2. Outputs drift toward the donor's meaning, and prompt or fine-tuning mitigations narrow but do not close the gap. A type-inference control where the answer is locally determined shows small, non-significant name effects.

claims.claim: Performance drops as identifier information is removed or made misleading, across models and tasks
claims.evidence: Tables 2-4 and Fig. 5 show a consistent Original > Perturbative > Anonymous > Confusing ordering across 9 models and 4 tasks; e.g., GPT-4o-mini code-doc accuracy 88.3 -> 79.7 -> 67.9, driven by true-positive rate. No CIs on the main tables, but deltas of 10-45 points on 600 samples far exceed sampling noise.

claims.claim: Misleading names steer outputs toward the donor's meaning, beyond an undirected drop
claims.evidence: Table 9: in two-choice selection, Confusing drops accuracy (GPT-3.5 92.8->52.4; others to 73-79%), while Anonymous barely moves 3 of 4 models. Fig. 6: donor-reference similarity exceeds random-pair similarity. The completion evidence is a single case study.

claims.claim: Lexical overemphasis persists under prompt-based and fine-tuning-based mitigations
claims.evidence: Fig. 8 and Table 11: perturbed examples, sanitize-by-renaming instructions and anonymized or mixed fine-tuning narrow the gap but leave Confusing below Original. Only 'representative' interventions were tried; no tool-augmented or execution-grounded intervention.

claims.claim: Naming effects are small when the answer is locally recoverable without the name
claims.evidence: Table 8: 317 ManyTypes4Py targets; changes of -3.2 to +2.2 pp, none significant after Holm; project-clustered CIs. Primitive types dominate, near ceiling.

claims.claim: The pattern holds for current LLMs
claims.evidence: The evaluated models are 2023-2024 generation (GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, GPT-4o-mini, Llama3-70B, DeepSeek-Coder-V2); the manuscript was submitted in September 2025. No 2026 frontier models, no agents, no repository context or tools.

patterns.note: Not an agent study. Snippet-level LLM comprehension is accurate on naturally named code but drops sharply, and in the donor's direction, when names are absent or misleading. Codebase question answering inherits this risk. Repository context, tools and current models were not tested.
text-embedding-3 code-search MRR 91.5 -> 72.2 (anonymous) -> 47.2 (confusing). Data-flow-aware GraphCodeBERT degrades less than CodeBERT. There is no lexical-retrieval baseline under renaming.
A weak hint that structure helps: GraphCodeBERT (data-flow attention) loses 15%/51% MRR vs CodeBERT's 22%/60% under anonymous/confusing naming. Single comparison.
Implication only: LLM-written summaries or explanations given to developers can follow stale or misleading names instead of the implementation. Not tested with developers.

methodology.sample: 600 CodeSearchNet samples (language not stated), HumanEval (Python) for completion, and 317 ManyTypes4Py targets from 217 projects for the type control
methodology.baselines: Original naming vs perturbative, anonymous and confusing renaming; dead-code insertion control for the external-identifier experiment
methodology.models: GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2, text-embedding-3, CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B; Llama-3.1-70B in the control
methodology.variance: No CIs or repeated runs for the main tables. The type-inference control uses project-clustered CIs and Holm-corrected McNemar tests.
methodology.ablations: Identifier type, external identifiers (with dead-code control), prompt interventions, anonymized and mixed fine-tuning, shuffling
methodology.contamination_controls: None. Contamination of CodeSearchNet and HumanEval is acknowledged as a threat.
methodology.languages: Python (HumanEval, ManyTypes4Py); CodeSearchNet subset language not stated

standards.peer_review: Under review at an ACM journal (submitted September 2025)
standards.artifacts: No code or data release link in the text

biases.detail: HumanEval and ManyTypes4Py are Python; the CodeSearchNet language is unstated.
Isolated snippets without repository context, documentation, callers or tool use (acknowledged as an ecological-validity limit).
Main-task results are single-run point estimates.
Public benchmarks likely present in pretraining corpora (acknowledged).
Conclusions about 'current LLMs' rest on 2023-2024 models; no reasoning or agentic models.
Face/Off transformation code and transformed datasets are not linked.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None favourably; commercial APIs used as test subjects

verdict_reason: A careful controlled design (AST-checked alpha-renaming, a donor-direction analysis, a type-inference boundary control with proper statistics, and candid threats-to-validity). The limits are snippet-level Python tasks, dated models, no variance on the main tables, and no artifacts. The direction of the effect is credible; its size for current tool-using agents on real repositories is unknown.
applicability: Relevant to an onboarding harness in which agents explain unfamiliar ingestion code to developers who lack domain knowledge. LLM explanations, summaries and embeddings lean on identifier names, and with misleading or stale names they describe what the code 'sounds like', not what it does. In a multi-repo Java estate with overloaded domain terms, agent-written walkthroughs, code cards and glossary entries should be checked against executed behaviour (tests, traces) or call and data-flow facts before they are stored as domain knowledge. Embedding search should also not be the only retrieval path for poorly named code. Whether current agents that read callers and run tests are still misled is untested, so treat this as a risk to verify, not a measured failure rate.
